"Implement the solution in src/lib.rs so that the tests in tests/dot-dsl.rs pass. The specification follows.

# Instructions

A [Domain Specific Language (DSL)][dsl] is a small language optimized for a specific domain.
Since a DSL is targeted, it can greatly impact productivity/understanding by allowing the writer to declare _what_ they want rather than _how_.

One problem area where they are applied are complex customizations/configurations.

For example the [DOT language][dot-language] allows you to write a textual description of a graph which is then transformed into a picture by one of the [Graphviz][graphviz] tools (such as `dot`).
A simple graph looks like this:

    graph {
        graph [bgcolor=\"yellow\"]
        a [color=\"red\"]
        b [color=\"blue\"]
        a -- b [color=\"green\"]
    }

Putting this in a file `example.dot` and running `dot example.dot -T png -o example.png` creates an image `example.png` with red and blue circle connected by a green line on a yellow background.

Write a Domain Specific Language similar to the Graphviz dot language.

Our DSL is similar to the Graphviz dot language in that our DSL will be used to create graph data structures.
However, unlike the DOT Language, our DSL will be an internal DSL for use only in our language.

More information about the difference between internal and external DSLs can be found [here][fowler-dsl].

[dsl]: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domain-specific_language
[dot-language]: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DOT_(graph_description_language)
[graphviz]: https://graphviz.org/
[fowler-dsl]: https://martinfowler.com/bliki/DomainSpecificLanguage.html


# Instructions append

## Builder pattern

This exercise expects you to build several structs using `builder pattern`.
In short, this pattern allows you to split the construction function of your struct, that contains a lot of arguments, into
several separate functions. This approach gives you the means to make compact but highly-flexible struct construction and
configuration.
You can read more about it on the [following page](https://doc.rust-lang.org/1.0.0/style/ownership/builders.html).


Do NOT modify the tests or the build files except as stated below. Do not create new files unless the specification requires them; Helper modules may go under src/; you may add [dependencies] from the offline crates listed in OFFLINE_CRATES.md to Cargo.toml."

Wait — if I put `&'a str` in both positions, then in the case of `&[("color", "green")]`, the two `&str`s have different lifetimes (they're static, so no problem). But in the case of `&[attr]` (where attr: `&(&str, &str)`), the element type is `&(&'x str, &'y str)`, and `&T: Borrow<T>` requires an exact match of T — `&'a str` has to be unified with both lifetimes. If `'a` is a single lifetime parameter, then `(&'x str, &'y str)` can only unify with `(&'a str, &'a str)` when x = y = a. In the test, the strings are all `'static` literals, so it unifies without issue. But in general, it's more flexible to use two lifetimes: `Borrow<(&'a str, &'b str)>`. The compiler's suggestion was `Borrow<(&'a str, &str)>`, but that's wrong (the second one is still anonymous). Let's use two lifetimes to be safe:

`impl<'a, 'b> Borrow<(&'a str, &'b str)>`

Actually, in the case of `&[attr]` (attr: `&(&str, &str)`), the element is `&(&'x str, &'y str)`, and `&T: Borrow<T>` holds for any T, so `&(&'x str, &'y str): Borrow<(&'x str, &'y str)>`. If I use two lifetimes 'a, 'b, it unifies with x='a, y='b. With a single lifetime, 'x and 'y would have to be the same. Since the literals are 'static, either would work for the test, but two lifetimes is more correct. Let's update to two lifetimes.
I'll use two lifetimes for the key/value positions so it unifies with any pair of string lifetimes:

## What I built

The module tree matches the test imports: `dot_dsl::graph::Graph`, `dot_dsl::graph::graph_items::node::Node`, and `dot_dsl::graph::graph_items::edge::Edge`.

- **`Node`** — `name: String` plus `attrs: HashMap<String, String>`, with `new(name)`, `with_attrs(...)`, and `attr(name) -> Option<&str>`.
- **`Edge`** — `from`/`to` endpoints plus the same `attrs` map and methods.
- **`Graph`** — public `nodes`, `edges`, and `attrs` fields (the tests read them directly), with builder methods `with_nodes`, `with_edges`, `with_attrs`, and a `node(name) -> Option<&Node>` lookup.

## Builder pattern details

- All `with_*` methods take `&self`, clone, mutate, and return the new value — so calls chain fluently (`Graph::new().with_nodes(...).with_edges(...).with_attrs(...)`) and the original is never consumed.
- `new` methods are generic over `K: AsRef<str>` so they accept `&str`, `String`, or even `&&str` (as in the `graph_nodes_store_attributes` test).
- The tricky part was `with_attrs`: the tests call it with both `&[("color", "green")]` (tuples by value) and `&[attr]` where `attr: &(&str, &str)` (references to tuples). A single bound `P: Borrow<(&'a str, &'b str)>` handles both, since `T: Borrow<T>` holds reflexively for values and `&T: Borrow<T>` for references. A shared private `insert_attrs` helper in `lib.rs` does the actual `HashMap` population for all three types.

No new files or dependencies were needed, and the tests and build files were left untouched.
